sketches.title: Word Gone Wrong
sketches.premise: You get a real obscure word and invent the most plausible definition for it. Make it sound useful, ordinary, and just slightly cursed; then the host reveals the truth and lovingly explains how badly you missed it.
sketches.criterion: The definition must keep the word's real meaning true enough that a reader could mistake your invention for a fair explanation of it.
sketches.move_shape: Write one dictionary-style definition under 90 characters, without using the word itself; example for “gobemouche”: “A person who believes every juicy story they hear.”
sketches.first_card: boustrophedon — a real word; give its plausible definition.

sketches.title: Word in the Wild
sketches.premise: A real obscure word lands in an everyday scene. Put it into a tiny bit of dialogue so naturally that nobody notices the strange word until the host explains what it really means.
sketches.criterion: The line must keep the obscure word used as a real word in a believable situation, with its grammatical role and basic sense intact.
sketches.move_shape: Write one spoken line under 90 characters containing the card word; example for “snollygoster”: “Don’t hire him—he’s a snollygoster in a cheap suit.”
sketches.first_card: petrichor — use this real word in a believable spoken line.

sketches.title: Two-Word Alibi
sketches.premise: Each obscure word comes with two ordinary nouns. Explain the strange word by connecting those nouns in one crisp claim, as if you are defending your guess in court. The host is your fond but merciless prosecutor.
sketches.criterion: The answer must preserve a clear, plausible relationship between both supplied nouns and the obscure word's real meaning.
sketches.move_shape: Write one claim under 90 characters using both nouns; example: “Umbrella + argument: a petty fight held under cover.”
sketches.first_card: kerfuffle — nouns: shoe, crowd; give your best one-line connection.

sketches.title: Definition Dating
sketches.premise: An obscure word is looking for its perfect plain-English match. Offer one short definition, then add a tiny warning label that makes your guess memorable without changing what the word means.
sketches.criterion: The plain-English definition must retain the word's real meaning; the warning may add tone but cannot contradict it.
sketches.move_shape: Write “It means ___; beware ___” under 90 characters; example for “ultracrepidarian”: “It means giving unwanted expert advice; beware the loud uncle.”
sketches.first_card: taradiddle — give its plain definition and a warning label.

sketches.title: Word as Evidence
sketches.premise: The host gives you a real obscure word and two everyday nouns. Write a fake piece of evidence—a note, label, sign, or text—that shows what the word means without defining it directly. Invented details are welcome; the meaning is not negotiable.
sketches.criterion: The evidence must make the word's real meaning inferable while keeping both supplied nouns present and relevant.
sketches.move_shape: Write one piece of evidence under 90 characters using both nouns; example: “Note: ‘The dog ate my homework again—classic kakistocracy.’”
sketches.first_card: eucatastrophe — nouns: wedding, cake; write one piece of evidence.

sketches.title: Word with a Catch
sketches.premise: You get a real obscure word and two familiar nouns. Turn them into a tiny rule, warning, or instruction that uses the word correctly, then add one playful consequence. The host checks the word first and laughs second.
sketches.criterion: The rule must use the obscure word in a way consistent with its real meaning, while both nouns remain part of the situation.
sketches.move_shape: Write one warning under 90 characters using both nouns; example: “No cat near the cake: that’s a recipe for a gallimaufry.”
sketches.first_card: apricity — nouns: bench, winter; write one playful warning.
